unit.unitTitle: What kind of garden would be best?
unit.unitOverview:
Hello! My name is Karim. I go to Ehel Academy with my friends Amal, Sami and Leila. We love gardens! In this unit, you can grow a garden too.

Do these with a grown-up. You can look, point, talk, draw, sort, count and tick. There are no marks. Just have fun and do your best.
learningPath: 5. Which garden do you like best?
unit.reviewStatus: Imported - Cambridge objective mapping still to be assigned

provenance.transformation: Adult-led Teacher & Parent Guide rewritten into learner voice for self-teaching

outcomes.text: 5. Which garden do you like best?

explainers.title: 1. Look at the garden
explainers.body:
Look at a garden with your grown-up. It can be a real garden, or a picture in a book. Point and say what you can see. Tick each thing when you find it.

Now say this little chant with your grown-up. Do the actions too!

We are digging. We are planting. We are watering. Plants grow in the sun!

explainers.title: 2. Draw a garden
explainers.body:
In the big box, draw a garden you have seen, or a garden you would like. You can draw someone in the garden doing something too.

Now tell your grown-up about your garden. Where is it? What grows in it?

explainers.title: 3. What grows in a garden?
explainers.body:
Some plants we can eat. Some flowers we just look at. Point to each one and say: do we eat it, or look at it?

Well done! Some plants, like the tomato and the beans, we can eat. The sunflower and the bright flower are lovely to look at.

headers: Eat it or look at it?

explainers.title: 4. What do plants need?
explainers.body:
A plant needs three things to grow big: the sun, some water, and good soil. Point to each word and say it out loud.

Now tick the three things a plant really needs. Careful, one of them is just for fun!

Did you tick the sun, the water and the soil? A plant does not need a football to grow!

explainers.title: 5. Which garden do you like best?
explainers.body:
There are different kinds of garden. Look at these three and think about each one.

Which garden do you like best? Point to it and tell your grown-up why. Then ask your family which one they like. Make a mark for each person to make a little chart.

Now count the marks. Which garden got the most? That one is the most popular!
bullets: Garden 1 grows food, like tomatoes and beans.
Garden 2 is full of flowers for the bees and butterflies.
Garden 3 is little pots by the door.

headers: Make a mark for each person

explainers.title: 6. Count the seeds
explainers.body:
Karim is planting seeds. Put some real seeds, or draw some seeds, in each cup. Then count them and say the number.

Which cup has the most seeds? Which cup has the fewest? Tell your grown-up.

explainers.title: Before you go
explainers.body:
You looked at gardens, sorted plants, and found out what plants need. Talk about these with your grown-up.

Well done! Now turn to the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet to plant a seed or design your own best garden.
bullets: What is one new thing you found out about gardens?
What are the three things a plant needs to grow?

bigIdeas.title: Look after your seed
lines: Remember, a plant needs the sun, water and soil.
Give it just a little water each day. Not too much!
Be patient. A seed sleeps for a few days before it wakes up and grows.
Look at your cup every day. One day, a tiny green shoot will push up through the soil. That means your seed has woken up and started to grow. How exciting!
When your plant starts to grow, draw it in the box. You can draw it again each week to see how much it has grown.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, ask your AI tutor: What does a bean seed need to grow?
Ask it to name one plant that grows well where you live.
Tell the tutor which plant you would like to grow.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up)
lines: With your grown-up, tell your AI tutor all about your garden.
Ask it: What is one thing you like about my garden?
Ask the tutor for one more plant you could grow next time.

speakingPrompts.title: Talk about it
lines: What can people do in a garden?
Have you ever helped in a garden? What did you do?

speakingPrompts.title: Talk about it with your grown-up
lines: What did you grow or draw?
What does a plant need to grow?
What was your favourite part of the project?
What creature would you like to visit your garden?
Would you like a garden at home one day?
Last of all, finish these two sentences out loud, or draw the answers.

grownUpGuide.label: For the grown-up
grownUpGuide.intro: This part is written for the parent or teacher sitting with the learner, and is kept in their own words.

sections.title: Before you begin
sections.body:
Hello, and welcome to this Global Perspectives project at Ehel Academy. This guide is written for you, the grown-up. In this subject, little children do not learn long lists of facts. Instead, they gently grow a few thinking-and-doing skills they will use all their lives: looking closely, talking and listening, choosing and saying why, and finding things out. This project grows those skills through a topic that five- and six-year-olds love: gardens and growing plants.

Your child is about five or six, so they are a pre-reader. That is exactly right. You read every part aloud, and your child looks, points, talks, draws, sorts, counts and plants. There is almost no writing. You do not need to be a gardener, and you do not need a big garden. You need a warm voice, a little time about twice a week, and a few simple things like some seeds, some soil and a cup.

sections.title: About this project: What kind of garden would be best?
sections.body:
Over this unit your child follows one big, friendly question: what kind of garden would be best? Along the way they look at real gardens, find out what grows in them, learn the few things a plant needs to grow, think about what makes a garden nice, and help plan a little garden. At the very end, your child plants a real seed in a cup, or draws their own best garden, or both.

The journey is broken into five short, picture-led little lessons, then a small final task, then a gentle look-back. Each little lesson is mostly looking and talking, with something to do with your hands. The garden is the fun part. The real learning is happening quietly underneath it.

sections.title: The little skills your child will grow
sections.body:
This project gently grows four Global Perspectives skills. Here they are in plain words, with what to listen for:

You will not test these skills or give marks. You simply give your child lots of friendly chances to practise them, and you notice out loud when they do them well. A warm 'What lovely looking, Karim!' teaches more than any worksheet.
items: Looking closely — noticing plants, colours, and the little creatures in a garden. Listen for: 'Look, a butterfly!' and 'This leaf is soft.'
Talking and listening — saying what they see and think, and hearing a friend's idea. Listen for: 'I can see ...' and 'What do you think?'
Choosing and saying why — picking a garden they like and giving a reason. Listen for: 'I like this one because ...'
Finding out — asking, looking, and wondering, such as what a seed needs to grow.

sections.title: How this unit works at Ehel Academy
sections.body:
Children of this age cannot study on their own, so this unit is led by you, the teacher or parent. Ehel Academy's youngest model has three parts that work together:

There is no rush and no fixed timetable. Spread the five little lessons across two or three weeks, or more. If your child loves planting the seed, plant three seeds. Curiosity is the goal.
items: You, the grown-up, leading the way. You read every part aloud, run the simple activities, and keep it warm and playful. Each little lesson is short, about 15 to 25 minutes, and you can split it into even smaller pieces.
Teacher sessions about twice a week. In these live sessions, children look at gardens together, sort pictures, plant seeds, and share their drawings with other learners.

A 24-hour AI tutor, used together with a grown-up. The tutor can read a lesson aloud, say a chant, ask your child a simple question, or tell a short plant story. At this age the tutor is always used with you sitting alongside, never alone.

sections.title: Meet Karim and his friends
sections.body:
So the lessons feel friendly, we follow a small group of children at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa. Your child can imagine playing right alongside them.

Together, Karim, Amal, Sami and Leila are a little garden team. As your child meets each new idea, they will see what Karim's friends do with it. Later, your child will do the very same things at home or in class.
items: Karim loves being outside. He is always asking 'why?' He once watched a tomato plant grow tall by his window.
Amal is calm and kind. She is very good at looking closely and helping her friends.
Sami has lots of energy. He loves digging in the soil and finding worms and other minibeasts.
Leila loves flowers and bright colours, and she likes to draw what she sees.

sections.title: How to run the five little lessons
sections.body: Each little lesson has the same simple shape: a short Aim (what it is for), a Talk about part (to get your child looking and talking), and a Do part (the hands-on bit). Read the Aim to yourself, then use the Talk about and Do parts with your child. Keep it light. Lots of talking is exactly right.

sections.title: Little lesson 2.1 - What is a garden?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child says what they already know about gardens, and meets the word garden.

Talk about. Ask: 'Have you ever seen a garden? What was in it? What can people do in a garden?' Let your child tell you all about it. Good answers might be: water the plants, dig, plant seeds, sit, smell the flowers, or play.

Do. Look at the garden pictures in the Activity Sheet together, or look at a real garden if you have one nearby. Point and say what you can see: a plant, a flower, a tree, soil, a watering can, a butterfly. Then say this little chant together and do the actions:

Finish by letting your child draw a garden they have seen, and tell you about it.
items: We are digging. (pretend to dig)
We are planting. (pretend to drop a seed)
We are watering. (pretend to pour)
Plants are growing in the sun! (reach up tall)

sections.title: Little lesson 2.2 - What grows in a garden?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child notices that gardens have plants we can eat and flowers we look at, and little creatures too.

Talk about. Ask: 'What grows in a garden near us?' Talk about the plants families grow here in East Africa, whether they live in Hargeisa, Mogadishu or Berbera: tomatoes, beans, herbs, maize, and trees like mango and papaya. Ask: 'Which of these have you tasted? Which is your favourite?'

Do. Play a simple sorting game. Name some garden plants and let your child put each one into a group: plants we can eat (tomato, beans, mango) or flowers we look at (sunflower, hibiscus). Then talk about the little creatures that visit a garden, such as butterflies, bees, ladybirds, and worms in the soil. Count how many creatures your child can name on their fingers.

sections.title: Little lesson 2.3 - What do plants need to grow?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child finds out that plants are living things, and that they need a few simple things to grow: sun, water and soil.

Talk about. Ask: 'Are plants alive, like us? What do you need to grow big and strong?' (Food, water, sleep.) Then ask: 'What do you think a plant needs?' Let your child guess.

Do. Together, name the three big things a plant needs, and do an action for each one: reach up for the sun, wiggle your fingers like falling water, and pat the ground for the soil. Then try a little planting: push a bean seed into a cup of soil, water it a tiny bit, and put it on a sunny windowsill. This is the start of your final task.

sections.title: Little lesson 2.4 - What kind of garden is best?
sections.body:
Aim. Your child sees that there are different kinds of garden, and begins to choose one and say why. They also find out what their friends like.

Talk about. Look at three kinds of garden together: a vegetable garden for growing food, a flower garden full of colour for bees and butterflies, and a tiny pot garden by the door. Ask: 'Which one do you like? Why?'

Do. Help your child see that the best garden depends on what you want. A hungry family might love the vegetable garden. Someone who loves butterflies might pick the flower garden. Someone with only a small step might choose the pots. Then do a little finding-out: ask three or four people 'Which garden do you like best?' and make a simple picture chart by putting a mark under each little garden. Count the marks together. Which garden is the most popular?

sections.title: Little lesson 2.5 - Let's plan our little garden
sections.body:
Aim. Your child plans a little garden, choosing what to grow and what to do in it, and practises working together kindly.

Talk about. Ask: 'If we made a garden at home or at Ehel Academy, what would we grow? What would we like to do in it?' Talk about growing food, watching butterflies, sitting to rest, or smelling flowers.

Do. Make a simple plan together on the Mini-Project sheet: tick the things to do in the garden, and draw the plants to grow. Then agree one kind garden rule for working together, such as 'we take turns with the watering can' or 'we are gentle with the plants'. Karim's group chose to grow tomatoes and sunflowers, with a little dish of water for the birds.

sections.title: Key words for this unit
sections.body: These are the words your child meets in this project. Say them often and warmly while you look and plant. There is no need to test them.

rows: A living thing that grows in the soil, like a flower or a tomato.
To get bigger, the way a seed turns into a plant.
A tiny thing that can grow into a plant.
The soft brown earth that plants grow in.
The warm, bright light that helps plants grow.
A drink that plants need to grow.
The pretty, colourful part of some plants.
A part of a plant we can eat, like a bean or a tomato.
A pretty creature with big wings that visits flowers.
A tiny creature like a bee, a worm or a ladybird.
Old food, like banana skin, that turns into food for the soil.
Thinking about what you will do before you do it.
The one you think is the very good choice for what you want.

sections.title: What you will need
sections.body: Nothing fancy. Gather these simple things before you start, and keep them together in a box:
items: A few seeds that grow quickly, such as beans. You can buy them cheaply at the market.
A cup or two, or a clean tin or an empty bottle cut in half, to plant in.
A little soil, and a small jug or bottle for water.
Some cotton wool (optional, so your child can watch a bean sprout).
Paper and crayons or coloured pencils for drawing gardens.
The Activity Sheet and the Mini-Project & Reflection sheet from this unit.

sections.title: Using the AI tutor together
sections.body:
At this age, the AI tutor is a helper you use side by side with your child, never a babysitter. Sit together, and let the tutor do the things a patient helper does well:

Whenever you see an Ask Your AI Tutor (with a grown-up) box in the children's sheets, that is your cue to open the tutor together. Keep it short and cheerful, and always stay in the room. If the tutor suggests something you would rather not do, simply skip it. You are in charge.
items: Read aloud. Ask it to read a little lesson or say the garden chant slowly, so your child can join in.
Ask a simple question. Ask it to ask your child one friendly question, then let your child answer out loud.
Tell a short story. Ask for a two-minute story about a seed growing into a plant.
Name a local plant. Ask it to name a plant that grows well where you live, so you can try it.

sections.title: The final task: plant a seed or design a garden
sections.body:
Everything leads to this. Your child, with you or in a small group, will either plant a real seed in a cup and look after it, or draw and label their own best garden. Many children love to do both. Then your child shows their plant or their picture to someone and tells them what they grew or drew, and why.

The full, child-friendly steps are in the separate Mini-Project & Reflection sheet. Your role is to gather a cup, some soil and a seed, to keep everything warm and patient, and to help only when your child is truly stuck. Remember that a small, wonky sprout your child cared for, or a bright, messy garden drawing they are proud of, is a complete success.

sections.title: Thinking about our work: a simple look-back
sections.body:
To finish, help your child look back and think about the project. Keep it gentle and spoken. The Mini-Project & Reflection sheet has happy and not-yet faces to point to, some stars to colour, and a few talking questions such as:

This looking-back is a real Global Perspectives skill, and it matters as much as the planting. When children hear that their looking, talking and caring are valued, not just a tidy plant, they learn the lesson that lasts.
items: What did you grow or draw?
What are the things a plant needs to grow?
Can you name one plant that grows where we live?
What was your favourite part of the garden project?
Would you like a garden at home one day?

sections.title: Keeping it warm and fun
sections.body: You now have everything you need. Go at your child's pace, get your hands in the soil together, and talk far more than you worry about getting it 'right'. If your child finishes this unit believing that they can look closely, choose a garden they like, and help a little plant grow, then the project has done its job beautifully. Have fun growing it, together.

project.title: Mini-project
project.intro:
This is the fun one! At Ehel Academy, Karim planted a seed and drew his best garden. Now it is your turn. With a grown-up, you can plant a little seed in a cup, or draw your own best garden — or do both! Take your time, and be gentle with your plant.

A garden takes time to grow, so this is a slow and happy project. Do just a little bit each day, and watch what happens.

steps.title: Plant a seed
steps.intro: A seed is tiny, but it can grow into a big plant. Let's plant one! Follow these steps with your grown-up, one at a time.
items: Get a cup, some soil, and a seed. A bean seed is a good one to start with.
Fill the cup with soil, almost to the top.
Push the seed into the soil, not too deep. Cover it gently.
Give it a little drink of water.
Put the cup on a sunny windowsill.
Water it a little bit every day, and watch it grow!

headers: Draw your plant when it grows

steps.title: Design your best garden
steps.intro:
Now dream up the best garden for you. First, make a little plan with your grown-up. Draw or tell the answers.

Now, in the big box, draw your best garden. Draw the plants and flowers. You can draw yourself in the garden too!

Would you like a bench to sit on, or a little path to walk on? You can draw those too. Then point to the parts of your garden and tell your grown-up all about it.

rows: What we will do in it
One creature we hope will visit

steps.title: Show and tell
steps.intro:
When your seed grows, or your garden picture is ready, show it to your family or your class. Tell them:

Sharing your garden makes people happy. Your family and friends will be so proud of what you did.
items: what you grew or drew
why you like it
what a plant needs to grow

assessment.note: Stages 1-3 are assessed through the mini-project and the look-back grid; the source pack ships no quiz.

selfAssessment.statement: I looked closely at a garden.
I can name a plant that grows.
I know a plant needs sun, water and soil.
I planted a seed or drew a garden.
